author: reek
body: ge-add and ge-double are the only Ed25519 operations that fail on the cross lanes, and the thing they do that fe-mul does not is rely on fe-add and fe-sub writing into their first argument and returning it. That contract has two halves: list-set-at writes in place and returns the same list, and arguments evaluate left to right. This file states both halves as answers a person can check.

author: reek
body: The expected values are the semantics the Developer's Guide records, not numbers read back off a backend.

author: reek
body: The fe-add shape: write into the first argument, return it.

author: reek
body: Appends its tag to a shared log and advances the log's cursor, which lives in slot 0. Two of these in one call record the order the two argument positions were evaluated in.

author: reek
body: list-set-at writes in place and hands back the same list, so the original binding sees the write. 1+2+3+4 becomes 11+2+3+4.

author: reek
body: And the returned list is the same object, not a copy, so both names report the same total.

author: reek
body: The fe-add contract: adding a copy of a list to itself doubles it and leaves the source alone. 1+2+3+4 = 10, doubled is 20, source still 10.

author: reek
body: Without the copy, add-into mutates its first argument while reading its second, which is the same list. Each limb is read after the earlier limbs were written, so this is the aliased shape ge-double relies on being left to right.

author: reek
body: Argument order, in one call with two mutating argument positions. Left to right records 7 then 9 and answers 79; right to left answers 97. fe-add and fe-sub depend on the former.
